title: The person who decides is not always the person who pays
hook: Adam Smith already worried about managers spending other people’s money. Jensen and Meckling turned that worry into a bill for agency costs.
body:
A principal hires an agent to act for them. A shareholder hires a manager. A patient hires a doctor. The agent usually knows more about what they did all day, and their interests are not the principal's. Effort is costly to the agent and valuable to the principal. Perks are pleasant to the agent and paid for by the principal. The gap is the agency problem.

Michael Jensen and William Meckling, in 1976, defined agency costs as the sum of three things: the cost of monitoring the agent, the cost of bonding (the agent's own efforts to commit, such as an audit they pay for), and the residual loss that remains because monitoring is never perfect. The firm, on their telling, is a knot of these contracts. It is not a person with a single goal. Smith's earlier complaint, that directors of joint-stock companies look after other people's money with less care than their own, is the same conflict in eighteenth-century dress.
deeper:
The remedies are all costly, which is why the problem does not disappear by being noticed. Paying the manager in shares aligns some incentives and can create others, including a taste for risk the diversified shareholder does not share. A board monitors, and then you have an agency problem between shareholders and the board. Publishing accounts helps outsiders and consumes time. None of these is a proof that managers are villains. They are the predictable result of asking one person to choose and another to bear the result, when the choice is hard to see.

The same pattern shows up outside firms: a voter and an elected official, a client and a lawyer. The name 'agency' is the economics. The structure is older than the name.
example: An owner-manager who keeps every extra dollar of profit will stay late if the late hour produces more than it costs them in fatigue. Hire a manager on a flat salary and the extra dollar goes to the owner, while the fatigue stays with the manager. The manager, left alone, stops earlier. A bonus tied to profit pulls the hour back out, but the owner now pays the bonus even in years when the profit came from luck rather than the late hour. That overpayment is part of Jensen and Meckling's residual loss. You can shrink it. You should not expect to invoice it down to zero.

sources.title: Jensen and Meckling, “Theory of the Firm” (1976), DOI 10.1016/0304-405X(76)90026-X
Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (Project Gutenberg)

review.notes: Agency costs are described as monitoring, bonding, and residual loss, which is Jensen and Meckling’s 1976 definition. The DOI is the Journal of Financial Economics paper. Smith is cited for the older joint-stock complaint, not as the inventor of the 1976 terms.
